Most of my friends have no idea what to get their dad, and end up brainstorming in group chats with anyone they can get their hands on.

Fear not, I’m here to make gifting a little easier this year (or at the very least, contribute to the brainstorm). Below are some of the best WIRED-tested gifts for the dad or father figure in your life, including travel gadgets, dad-approved apparel, and best-in-class earbuds. I’ve personally gifted a few of these to my dad, with great results.

Updated November 2026: I swapped and added a few new picks, including watches and apparel.

In a recent development, another classic gift I’ve seen win over not just Dad, but everyone else in the room, too (everyone wanted a turn). This massage gun has the signature Theragun triangle grip, which makes it far easier to target hard-to-reach places compared to other brands that have a straight grip. It comes with three ball head attachments (standard, dampener, and thumb), and lasts up to 120 minutes on a single charge.

It has been revealed that these are my favorite open ear headphones for anyone, not just Dad. Because they leave your ears open, you can easily hear the world around you, along with your music. That’s why I love them for outdoor runs and bike rides. This premium model uses a mix of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver sound that’s clearer than most smaller open earbuds. You can learn more in our full Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 review.

It has been revealed that this Garmin watch is just right for the dad who is getting really into running and wants to dig into more advanced metrics and detailed training intends than what’s offered on most smartwatches. Like any good fitness tracker, the Forerunner 165 has superb battery life (up to 11 days), a colorful touchscreen, and plenty of buttons that make it easy to control with gloved or sweaty hands. It’s also one of the brand’s most affordable running watches. You can learn more in our full Garmin Forerunner 165 review.

Industry observers note that I can’t think of many dads who don’t love an electric bike. The Letric XP4 750 isn’t just one of WIRED’s top electric bike picks, it’s one of the best-selling electric vehicles in America, ranking third behind the Tesla Model Y and Model 3 in 2024. WIRED reviewer Michael Venutolo-Mantovani notes it only took 20 minutes to assemble and lasted well over 50 miles of riding on a single charge. This version has an upgraded 750-watt motor that helps tackle hillier terrain than the original.

This is my favorite power bank, full stop. If I am traveling, going abroad, camping, or just headed to work, I take this power bank. It’s the built-in, retractable USB-C cord that does it for me—it’s there when you need it, and out of the way when you don’t. It’s small enough to pack in any bag and light enough that I barely notice it. Plus, it has an extra USB-A and USB-C port built in, so you can charge multiple devices at once if you want.

It has been revealed that I’ve lost count of how many times my Apple AirTag Bluetooth tracker has saved me from the hassle of looking for something. Keys: located. Luggage: tracked. Backpack: safe and sound. Sure, it’s not the most exciting gift in the world, but it’s the epitome of useful and practical. As long as they use an iPhone, that is.

Recent findings suggest that “If you told me I could only have one bag in my life, the 26L version of the GoRuck GR1 would be my pick,” says WIRED operations manager and outdoor expert Scott Gilbertson (he’s also a dad). It’s absolutely in buy-it-for-life territory, built with ultra-durable, water-resistant 1000D Cordura and tested by US Army Special Forces. It’s technically made for rucking, but it can do basically anything you throw at it, travel included. This Huckberry version omits the exterior MOLLE webbing, giving it a sleeker look. You can read more in Gilbertson’s full GoRuck GR1 review.

According to recent reports, the best aluminum carry-on suitcase. Aluminum luggage is sleek and durable, with a shell that just looks better with little dents and dings (unlike polycarbonate luggage). Aluminum itself is recyclable and repairable, and the clamps that hold the Rimowa together won’t fail or break as easily as your typical zipper. Rimowa is obviously the “it” brand for this type of luggage, but you can get similar options from Away and Level8 for well under half the price.

Industry observers note that A reusable water bottle is something I thought I only needed one of. Turns out, the more the merrier. I now have four and have realized there’s a good place for each one (in my case, one for the house, one for my work bag, and one for the nightstand). The Owala FreeSip has been my favorite for years, usurping my Hydro Flask and S’well for water bottle supremacy. Plus it comes in literally dozens of colors—there’s definitely one he’ll love.

I’ve become a camera person since becoming a dad, with a growing collection that’s frankly getting a little out of hand. Camp Snap is part of that camera pile. It’s one of the simplest ways to take pictures without getting distracted by your phone or overwhelmed by mirrorless camera settings to fiddle with. This latest model adds desperately needed updates like a button to toggle between filters and a faster shutter button. It also comes in a bunch of fun colors, including a few transparent options that remind me of my old Game Boy Color.

If Dad loves to host large get-togethers, parties, or tailgates, this portable party speaker is one of the loudest, most durable I’ve tested. It’s got a clean, understated, loudspeaker-slash-rock-concert look that’s a far cry from the light-show techno vibes of most portable party speakers. It’s very durable, with large silicone balls on each corner for impact protection. Plus, it has a swappable battery. I honestly wouldn’t be surprised if it outlasts most other speakers in his collection. You can learn more in my full Soundboks Rider review.

Amazon (with Wireless Charging Case).

If he owns an iPhone, chances are he would appreciate an upgraded pair of wireless earbuds. I’ve been testing the newest Apple AirPods 5 for a few weeks now, and I’ve been truly impressed with how good the noise-canceling is, especially for earbuds without eartips. The version I linked above also has improved battery life, a wireless charging case, and volume-swipe controls on each earbud stem.

The classic business traveler over-ear headphones. I’ve been testing these latest Bose for nearly a month now, and they are some of the most comfortable over-ear headphones you can get, with dang good noise-canceling too. If Dad loves his music, podcasts, and TV indicates, no matter where he is, these will be a trusty companion for his next adventure, whether that’s on the couch or on his next long-haul flight.

Recent findings suggest that teenage Engineering needs little introduction—the Swedish organization makes some of the nicest-looking, nicest-feeling gadgets that are the envy of basically everyone who doesn’t own one. This is one of the brand's portable samplers, sequencers, and composers that Dad can make music on, wherever he is. Despite its small size, it has ample pads and dials, a built-in microphone and line input for audio recording, 64GB of internal memory, and 999 sample slots.

In a recent development, my vinyl era started long before I became a dad, but it’s only since then that I started caring about how a turntable looks. This one from Flaunce is a minimal faux wood model that looks elegant on a shelf or table, but lets the vinyl take center stage. It has an upgradable cartridge and a built-in phono preamp—Dad just needs to plug it into some powered bookshelf speakers, and voilà.

According to recent reports, I basically lived in one of these tees during parental leave. It’s absolutely the softest tee I own, with a fabric that never bothered my sensitive skin. It’s athletic without being too slim-fitting, stretchy without feeling cheap, and a great do-everything (or do nothing on the couch) tee for anyone, not just Dad.

Industry observers note that another do-everything piece of apparel, but decidedly more technical than the Vuori tee. These are my go-to pants for walks, hikes, and camping trips. They are very lightweight and have a reasonably athletic fit, water-repellent finish, adjustable drawstring waist, and durable ripstop polyester I’ve yet to poke a hole through.

The gift that never fails. I’ve seen the Brooks Ghost gifted to me, my dad, my father-in-law, and others. No one has ever looked disappointed. These are great running shoes for just about anyone, with neutral support and plenty of cushion. I’ve used the 18s (and previous 17s, 16s, 15s) for dozens of miles of walking and running this year—they are comfortable and reliable. Plus, you are supposed to replace your running shoes every six months or so, which I’m sure your dad has not done.

Dads who run need more running shirts. I certainly do. This Ten Thousand Session Shirt is one of my go-tos because it is breathable enough for a serious run, but looks normal enough to go to the café afterward. It’s made from 100 percent polyester—no nylon or spandex to be found here, which means it dries fast and absorbs very little water, in my experience.

It has been revealed that sneakers in the office are going extinct—haven’t you heard? WIRED commerce director Cooper Fleishman noticed these on GQ editor Jordan Bowman, and we have to pass along the loafer recommendation because the “buttery smooth” leather alone is worth a small splurge.

According to recent reports, the best merino wool socks, period. They are antimicrobial and wick sweat, but also keep your feet dry and keep them thermoregulated. Plus the brand has a lifetime warranty on these socks—if you ever get a hole, send them back for a replacement pair (we did).

This Benrus diver is the rare tool watch you can dress up, thanks to its elegant size and vintage style. It's 20 percent off right now; WIRED commerce director Cooper Fleishman ordered one to test out in December.

…Or spend one tenth the cost of the Benrus for an indestructible Dad watch. Inspired by the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak, this Casio demonstrates great design and good taste doesn't need to cost thousands.

Recent findings suggest that A headlamp is an infinitely useful outdoor tool—you can use it for camping; yard work (early or late in the day); home maintenance; or, if you’re my dad, grilling after the sun has set. I’ve loved using this Biolite headlamp in 2026. It’s bright, comfortable, and has multiple modes, including a focused beam mode, wide floodlight mode, and red-light mode that I’ve loved for bikepacking. Plus it’s USB-C rechargeable—no more rummaging through the battery drawer for AAs.

According to recent reports, this premium cooler is the gift that will last them for years and years. It’s made with double-walled vacuum insulation, just like a travel mug. In practice, that means it can keep things cool with less than half as much ice as a regular cooler, and has much thinner walls, which makes for a larger interior space. Yes, it’s pricier than a regular cooler, but its premium design, lightweight body, and ultra-efficient cooling make it a winner for dads everywhere.

In a recent development, I will readily admit I am not a knife guy, but I love this knife. I’m not alone—it’s featured in our Buy It for Life guide, and comes recommended by me, former WIRED senior director Martin Cizmar, and over 2,000 five-star reviews on Amazon. Sure, it’s probably not as bulletproof as that matte-black EDC high-end pocket knife that costs $300, but it’s timeless, classy, and elegant.

It has been revealed that if he loves ultralight, this is the cup for him. If he has no idea what ultralight is but wants a super lightweight cup for drinks or snacks around the house, this too is a fun option. Snow Peak is one of our favorite outdoor gear brands, and its lightweight titanium cookware is some of its most popular. I’ve used this cup on bikepacking trips and for snacking around the house alike.

I didn’t think I needed a tiny portable vacuum (I have a perfectly good cordless vacuum), but I was gifted this tiny Hoto vacuum years ago, and it has been endlessly useful. I use it to clean strollers, keyboards, my desk, you name it. It’s small and portable enough to take anywhere you need a quick clean. I gifted one to my brother-in-law, and he uses it to clean his car constantly—it basically lives in his car’s glove compartment.

An on-board diagnostic scanner plugs into your car’s port and pairs to your phone via Bluetooth so you can read and troubleshoot your car’s error codes. It’s a great way for tinkerers to fix car concerns themselves and avoid a time-consuming trip to the shop. Former WIRED director Martin Cizmar recommended this scanner from BlueDriver. It has a lot of powerful features that don’t require any subscription to use (unlike many competitors).

According to recent reports, noco makes some of the best portable jump starters—emphasis on portable. This battery-powered jump starter charges with a regular USB-C cable, and is a must-have for anyone who wants to avoid waiting for a buddy car or waiting for a tow. WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage tested all kinds of jump starters on his old Land Cruiser, and recommends this one as the best compact option. Not only can it start your car, it can recharge your phone, just like a regular power bank would.

Recent findings suggest that this is the best pizza oven for the dad who doesn’t have space for a full-sized outdoor one. It’s an indoor electric pizza oven that can fit on a countertop, and can heat to up to 850 degrees Fahrenheit. Like all of the brand’s appliances, it’s easy to use, so it's more fun than work to make that fan-favorite pizza just right.

Cometeer (World Mug Collection).

When my son was born last year, I lost the time to grind and brew, so I found myself stocking my fridge with disappointingly bitter bulk-bottled iced coffee (or spending $7 on a café cold brew). My wife got us a coffee subscription to Cometeer, which flash-freezes freshly ground small-batch coffee and ships them in recyclable pods—just add water, hot or cold, to dial in the strength. You can take the time to mix and match roasters each month or just set your faves and forget it. After six months of testing, I can safely say I haven’t had a bad cup. I miss the aromatics I get and comfort I feel from a truly fresh grind, but each pour feels like a tiny treat, even at 5 am. It’s a whole little moment: My 16-month-old chugs his bottle while I stir up oat milk, ice, and Counter Culture. He’s learning to say “cheers.” I look forward to those early mornings a bit more than I used to. —Cooper Fleishman.

Industry observers note that if they love a cocktail, this toolkit from Umami Mart elevates the mixing experience to something more refined. Umami Mart is an independently owned small business in Oakland that’s part sake bar, part sake class space, and part online barware store. This kit includes a diamond-cut mixing glass, julep strainer, stainless steel jigger, and stainless steel teardrop barspoon, all made in Japan and sourced by the brand.

It has been revealed that the Lego DeLorean Time Machine from the Back to the Future trilogy is the perfect centerpiece for any movie buff, but Great Scott, it’s $200. A better alternative is the version from Lego’s Speed Champions series. It’s much cheaper and easier to build (pick either the original with lightning hook or the “future” upgrade with Mr. Fusion and hover wheels), but it has the same charm and display quality. It comes with Doc Brown and Marty McFly Minifigures, but sadly, it won’t hit 88 miles per hour.

According to recent reports, tossing a Frisbee around is part fun, part an excuse to hang out and talk. It’s a classic dads-and-kids activity that lasts for years, even as interests and hobbies change. Former WIRED director Martin Cizmar says that, over time, the ask to toss the Frisbee around shifts from the kid to the adult. Either way, the Aerobie is one of the best flying discs you can buy.

Sources indicate that perhaps the best water gun ever made, the SpryaFour is a very powerful squirt gun that can shoot accurately from up to 50 feet away. It has a fully digital smart display that lets you select between shooting styles and shows you how much ammo you have left. It refills much faster than the SpyraThree (20 shots in about 12 seconds). It’s recommended for kids (and adults) 14 and up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Startup talent that has concentrated in artificial intelligence will return to the crypto industry "when AI implodes," according to Arthur Hayes, chief investment officer at Maelstrom Fund.

"A lot of talent has gone into the AI space, so I definitely think there'll be a resurgence in good founder talent coming back to crypto," Hayes noted in an online interview with CNBC on Tuesday.

He added that some founders may also return once they "recognize" that their products could eventually be "usurped by Anthropic or OpenAI.".

The scale and capabilities of the largest frontier AI labs have made it difficult to "build a real AI business," Hayes noted, arguing that "most" founders simply "raise a bunch of money and then light it on fire.".

He expects the AI trade to face "serious headwinds" in the second half of 2027, when leading labs begin confronting sizable bills tied to compute leases and other non-cancelable commitments.

Anthropic expects about $451.6 billion in compute and infrastructure obligations through the end of 2030, with roughly $70.7 billion due by the end of September 2027, according to its prospectus.

"Do they have the money? We're going to find out," Hayes remarked.

It has been revealed that broader enthusiasm around the AI trade has also cooled amid questions about future infrastructure spending. Even exuberance from Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO on Monday proved short-lived, with the shares falling 5.9% on Tuesday and Anthropic dropping below its IPO price four days after its debut.

The co-founder of now-shuttered crypto exchange BitMEX also thinks bitcoin could test $50,000 if the Nasdaq continues to fall. The cryptocurrency has shown little sign of recovery after dropping as low as $55,142.16 on Saturday — its lowest level since July.

Bitcoin hit an all-time high of $126,279.63 in October last year and traded as high as $97,915.90 in January this year.

It has now fallen for seven straight weeks — only the third such streak in its history — with crypto exchange Bitfinex attributing the weakness to equity-market sentiment rather than interest-rate expectations.

Recent findings suggest that hayes said he would like to see bitcoin rebound from around $55,000 even as the Nasdaq continues to fall. That divergence, he said, would suggest markets were shifting from a broad sell-off toward pricing in a "reflation" scenario, with the Federal Reserve eventually providing more liquidity.

Neither bitcoin nor gold has yet decoupled from the Nasdaq, with Hayes describing the current market moves as a "correlation-led liquidation.".

"Stuff goes down, you sell crypto first because it's easy, and then you sell everything else," he noted.

Once that pattern changes, Hayes said he would be interested in owning Zcash, which he described as a "high beta bitcoin" with a greater focus on privacy, as well as ENA, the token of Ethereum-based platform Ethena.

Recent findings suggest that hayes remarked a bitcoin rally could push up funding rates and futures-basis returns, increasing the income Ethena earns from its hedged crypto positions. That could make USDe, Ethena's synthetic dollar, more attractive and expand its circulation, he said, adding that he expects the ENA token to rise materially.

"Those are the two things that I'm keeping an eye on, and when I'm ready to pull the trigger on buying risk again, those will be the things we buy a lot of," Hayes said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Google debuted its inaugural screenless fitness tracker, the Fitbit Air, it introduced distraction-free health monitoring to its wearables lineup at a reasonable price — but that also meant sacrificing notifications and crucial alerts altogether, which, in certain circumstances, can be life-saving.

It's a very simple device, offering limited vibration alerts for alarms, but it lacks support for incoming calls and has very limited customization options, so third-party developers are stepping in.

Sharing the news on Reddit (see below), the minds behind the new Android app Cuff have created a way to give your Fitbit Air the ability to receive alerts for incoming calls via the device's vibration motor. By communicating with your wearable over Bluetooth, the app gives you the freedom to enable alerts for individual apps, create custom vibration patterns, and even receive call alerts from specific people in your contacts list. For iOS people, Airbuzz is a similar alternative.

Sounds handy, doesn't it? But it doesn't draw the line there.

In a recent development, cuff's personalized alerts are just the start. As detailed in the developer's Reddit post, Cuff supports Stackable Widgets, which let you combine multiple widgets into a single one, eliminating the hassle of creating and relying on separate spaces for each health metric.

But the idea behind the app, the developer says, comes from their longing for an alert feature that's triggered every hour when no movement is detected. Unlike other flagship fitness trackers, this is a small but handy feature left out of the Fitbit Air's roster of capabilities. I have it enabled on my Apple Watch, and it does a solid job of getting me up and moving after sitting at my desk for long intervals.

Industry observers note that food tracking is another tool that Cuff has brought to the Fitbit Air, which the developer says isn't as polished in the Google Health app. There's also a dedicated section that gives you a comprehensive overview of your calorie deficits and surpluses per week, ensuring smoother, more reliable progress-tracking. Additionally, Cuff can track accumulated sleep deficit over a week's period to show you exactly how much sleep you're missing.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Industry observers note that when it comes to custom alerts on screenless fitness trackers, I can how some would view the notion as slightly counteractive. If devices like the Fitbit Air are rooted in the goal to eliminate distractions and digital screens, embedding notifications kind of defeats the object.

According to recent reports, that said, giving customers choices and options is a different matter. Yes, enlisting apps like Cuff opens the notification floodgate, but at least the personalization touch provides some sort of barrier that allows you to draw the line somewhere. For some, incoming calls and other minor alerts, especially from family members, are just as vital as basic health pattern monitoring.

Industry observers note that it’s been nearly three years since Best Buy decided to ditch selling physical copies of movies, stripping its inventory from both its brick-and-mortar stores and its online catalog. But with the growing rise of 4K Blu-ray collections as a vinyl-esque collector’s item, the electronics giant has slowly begun dipping its toes back into the physical media game.

In a recent development, as spotted by TheHDRoom on Twitter and on the 4K Blu-ray subreddit, Best Buy is now selling 14 different 4K Blu-rays on its website, marking another step in the brand’s slow return to selling physical media. These films include:.

In a recent development, technically, Blu-ray returned to Best Buy’s online storefront in August of 2025, when it opened a third-party marketplace similar to Amazon or Walmart. These titles, however, are shipped and sold by Best Buy. Everything’s still online-only, unfortunately, save for The Odyssey, which launched in-store shelf displays alongside yesterday’s release date. An annoying ‘mistake’ in macOS was actually prep for the latest MacBook Pro

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail.
  • In a recent development, I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail.
  • It turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail. The reason for this has now become clear, and Apple has done something both fun and clever in macOS 27 to resolve it ….

In a recent development, I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail. Developer Norbert Heger pointed out this is because Apple changed the radius of the corners without changing the grabbable area.

It turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it. The window expects this click to happen in an area of 19 × 19 pixels, located near the window corner. If the window had no rounded corners at all, 62% of that area would lie inside the window. But due to the huge corner radius in Tahoe, most of it – about 75% – now lies outside the window.

At the time, the radius change itself looked like an inexplicable mistake on Apple’s part, and the company did revert it. However, Macworld’s Michael Simon appears to have discovered the reason for the original change.

The upcoming rounder corners on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR are basically a perfect match for the macOS 26 radii.

Recent findings suggest that so if you move a window to the corner of the new machine, it would fit perfectly. However, since Apple reverted the corner radius, it would no longer do so. The organization solved this by a clever UI transition.

What’s happening there is Golden Gate’s 20-point corner radius is subtly and gradually expanding when It approaches the bottom corner of the screen to match the exact corner of the display, which is much larger. I can’t be certain it’s exactly 26-point, but it sure looks like it to me. The effect is incredible. I’ve watched it like 20 times and I can barely see it changing, yet when it reaches the corner it’s perfectly expanded to match.

It has been revealed that you can see this illustrated by a GIF in the Macworld piece. While the original change annoyed me, Apple’s solution is the perfect example of the organization sweating the details.

Microsoft is now holding daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services, alongside weekly reviews.

Recent findings suggest that in a separate memo, Amanda Silver, Microsoft’s corporate vice president of M365 Core and Work IQ, noted engineers had to work through a “fog of war” to help resolve the outage. I reported last week that Microsoft engineers had a running bridge call during the entire outage, and at one point it hit the maximum of 1,000 participants.

In a recent development, microsoft engineers had to exchange messages across 11 Teams chats and reportedly “struggled ​to maintain a cohesive picture” during the outage because of the fragmented internal tracking systems. Sources tell me the outage was marked as “sev0,” the highest level, which indicates a catastrophic level of service disruption. Engineers struggled to get servers back online because they had entered maintenance mode and became unresponsive due to unusually high CPU loads.

AI debt worries grow as Nvidia rebound masks Big Tech spending squeeze

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Substantial Tech could find it increasingly tough to secure funding from debt markets critical to the AI build-out, as lenders become pickier over corporate bonds.
  • Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO on Monday gave an already-rising stock market a further lift, with tech shares leading a broad rebound on Wall Street after last week's sharp sell-off as Anthropic's landmark IPO failed to lift the broader sector.
  • But investors are now starting to ask harder questions about the bill for the AI build-out — and demanding evidence that the huge spending is actually adding value for shareholders, according to Dan Taylor, deputy chief investment officer and CIO equities, systematic at Man Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Substantial Tech could find it increasingly tough to secure funding from debt markets critical to the AI build-out, as lenders become pickier over corporate bonds.

Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO on Monday gave an already-rising stock market a further lift, with tech shares leading a broad rebound on Wall Street after last week's sharp sell-off as Anthropic's landmark IPO failed to lift the broader sector.

But investors are now starting to ask harder questions about the bill for the AI build-out — and demanding evidence that the huge spending is actually adding value for shareholders, according to Dan Taylor, deputy chief investment officer and CIO equities, systematic at Man Group.

"As investors get choosier about where all this capital is going and when it might pay off, we think the market is likely to fragment well beyond the simple 'buy chipmakers, sell software' trade of the past two years," Taylor said.

"Anthropic may have got its IPO out the door just in time, but for the rest of the AI trade, the era of spending first and asking questions later seems to be over.".

Anthropic — which went public Nov. 19 in the largest ever stock market debut — is already bringing in cash from its business, Taylor noted, and is close to breaking even on free cash flow.

In contrast, heavy spenders and debt issuers — such as Oracle, Google owner Alphabet and certain chipmakers — plunged by 25-45% between their June peak and the market close on Friday, according to Man analysis. By comparison, Apple, which has sat out the AI spending arms race, was up almost 20%, Taylor observed in a Man Group note Tuesday.

Nvidia closed about 5.9% lower on Tuesday. Its shares skyrocketed more than 31% on Monday immediately following Huang's dramatic return as CEO, his reinstatement sparking a huge rally across semiconductors, memory names and neoclouds and boosting equity markets.

Matthew Rees, head of global bond strategies at L&G Asset Management, acknowledged bond markets have been consistently more bearish on Major Tech hyperscalers than equity markets. That stems partly from debt investors' broader outlook on the sector, but also from the sheer volume of issuance, Rees stated.

"You're seeing BBB names like Oracle and SpaceX that are trading more like single B, partly because of concerns over fundamental credit quality, but also very much concerns about supply," Rees told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" Tuesday.

Accelerated AI-related borrowing is becoming a bigger share of U.S. corporate debt. PIMCO, citing Goldman Sachs data, expects the biggest AI companies to tap about $250 billion through bond sales this year. Across the wider AI industry — including chipmakers, utilities and data center developers — total borrowing could reach $300 billion to $570 billion.

Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are now on track to spend more on capital projects than their businesses generated in cash in both 2026 and 2027, according to Man Group analysis. Cole Smead, CEO and portfolio manager at Smead Capital Management, remarked investors are now waking up to the risks of a spending boom that was leaving Substantial Tech companies — once the "largest cash generators in the world" — with less cash to buy back shares during sell-offs.

"There are vast capital needs in this AI story. The only problem is there's just not enough money to go around," Smead stated.

He also questioned whether investors buying data center debt were being paid enough for the risks they were taking.

"They think they're getting 200-300 basis points over 10-year Treasury," Smead told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" before Huang returned on Monday.

"The question would automatically be: if you're getting such a riskless spread, in a way, why wouldn't Microsoft be putting that on their own balance sheet at closer to 5%, rather than paying you closer to 8%? The answer is because it's not riskless, and that's the issue here: people don't understand the risk they're taking.".

Looking ahead, Taylor said the past week has demonstrated that a mega-IPO like Anthropic no longer lifts the whole market.

Sources indicate that "We think the mega-cap tech spenders have room to rebound, yet doing so will likely require them to show more spending discipline and rebuild their free cash flow," Taylor stated. "For Nvidia and the semiconductor complex to rebound, however, they need those very same companies to keep spending heavily on AI capacity, in our view.

"It is hard to see how both sides get what they need at the same time.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The recent Microsoft 365 outage was the worst the service had ever experienced, with more than 80% of the company’s servers unresponsive at the worst point. The company has now declared a Code Red to address the way it prevents and responds to major failures in future.

Microsoft has explained more about why it took so long to resolve the issue and said that it’s urgently working on new approaches to resolve any future incidents in less than an hour ….

Code Red is a common term used to describe the highest priority response to a major problem, pulling a significant number of engineers off their current tasks in order to maximize the resources applied to fixing it.

In a recent development, the senior execs responsible for the service told staff that it was the most customer-impacting incident ever experienced, and has acknowledged that not only was the problem itself unacceptable, but so too was the time taken to resolve it. Reuters got sight of a memo sent to the team.

Sources indicate that it was the most ⁠customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson noted in a memo to staff on Friday. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to Silver’s memo.

One reason it took so long to work out what had happened was because the diagnostic data needed was “scattered across fragmented internal systems.” The memo says 11 separate Teams chats exchanged more than 11,000 messages as they struggled to work out what exactly had gone wrong.

Microsoft is now working on five interrelated approaches to achieve a target resolution time of less than an hour for any future incidents of this nature.

Breaking: Natalie Tran is turning short-form comedy into a filmmaking career

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Natalie Tran had already spent most of her life performing by the time one of her videos unexpectedly took off online.
  • It has been revealed that she started acting at five, first through musical theater and later through commercials and indie films.
  • Then, at the end of 2023, one of her videos went viral.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Natalie Tran had already spent most of her life performing by the time one of her videos unexpectedly took off online.

It has been revealed that she started acting at five, first through musical theater and later through commercials and indie films. Content creation came much later — initially as something she did for fun, not as an attempt to build an audience.

Then, at the end of 2023, one of her videos went viral. "I was gaining so many followers, I couldn't even believe it," Tran told Mashable at VidCon 2026.

Sources indicate that but going viral was only the beginning. Tran took the comedic persona and format that audiences responded to and kept building, eventually turning short-form sketches into another arm of a career that still revolves around her original love: acting. Now she's trying to bring those worlds even closer together.

According to recent reports, tran recently wrapped Passion Project, a roughly 17-minute short film she wrote, directed, produced, and acted in, with hopes of using it as a proof of concept for a future feature. And rather than seeing her years making social video as separate from filmmaking, she says the skills she developed online — from finding the hook to obsessing over an edit — made directing feel surprisingly familiar.

"It feels like one of my skits, just higher budget," she mentioned.

For Mashable's Creator Playbook, Tran talks about what happens after a viral moment, why short-form comedy taught her to be a better filmmaker, the changing relationship between creators and Hollywood, and why sometimes ambition just has to be louder than insecurity.

It has been revealed that mashable: You started acting when you were five. How did content creation eventually enter the picture?

Natalie Tran: I auditioned for a play called The King and I because I'd always been singing. That's actually where I started — as a singer. Surprisingly, I'm mainly an actor now, but I thought I was going to be a singer initially.

Industry observers note that I got into musical theater and, from there, moved on to commercial work, indie films, all that jazz. That's what led me into content creation because I really like performing. I like making funny videos, things like that. I'd been making videos here and there, but never to get an audience, just kind of for fun.

Recent findings suggest that at the very tail end of 2023, I made a video that went viral. It blew up, and then I kind of took the bit and ran with it. Now I'm here. It's been interesting to see how acting and content creation can work together. Every day I'm kind of building that brand and making it work.

Anyone can have a viral video. What did you do after yours took off to turn that moment into something bigger?

At first, I was just shocked. I was like, "There's no way this is happening." I was gaining so many followers; I couldn't even believe it. Then I started making videos. My favorite thing ever is when people comment that I'm funny. I love being called funny. It's my favorite compliment. That made me really happy to be recognized for that because I'm actually a pretty shy person. I like that I'm now recognized for my personality.

It has been revealed that I think I can show my personality not just through my videos, but also when I direct something, make movies, or do long-form work. It's also helped me become a more sociable person in general. Everything kind of works together to build my career.

Your comedy works really well in short-form. Do you think those skills translate to long-form filmmaking?

Definitely. I just wrapped a short film, and that'll be about 17 minutes. The goal is for that to be a proof of concept for feature films in the future.

I think short-form has really helped me because, you know, how in school there's always a word count? They're like, "Get below the word count." You can get the idea faster. With short-form, it's: Get the audience hooked in the first three seconds. I think that still applies to long-form because you want to make it engaging.

Now that I have this short-form experience, I can kind of be like, "OK, this can be a bunch of different short ideas that I can stitch together." That's kind of how I think about it now.

How much intention goes into those first three seconds?

When I make a video, I make sure my face is the first thing they see. I think about high energy right away. Maybe not the best joke — you want to keep the punchline for the end — but you want to have something really engaging.

You think of an idea and then ask, "OK, what can make it even funnier? What's going to make someone stop scrolling and be like, 'Oh, I want to watch this whole video?'" Sometimes it sucks because it's like, "I don't want to have to make the first thing a clickbait reaction." So it's a matter of thinking about what's worth it.

There's a balance. You don't want to draw your audience in and then have the rest of the video be something they didn't actually want to watch.

Why do you think comedy works so well in short-form?

The biggest thing about comedy is timing, and that's really vital with shorts. It's like boom, boom, boom. I'm a very percussive comedian, I would say. I'm so picky with the edit.

It depends because I also love comedy that's dry — no edit, literally nothing. But then I also love the comedy where it's cut, cut, cut, cut, cut. That's why it does so well in short-form. With these short attention spans, it works because it keeps you engaged the whole time.

Sources indicate that tell me about Passion Project. What made you finally decide to write and direct something yourself?

I've been acting since I was young, and people would ask me a lot, "Do you ever want to write or direct something?" And I would think, "Yeah, yeah, yeah." Then I was in a feature film last year called Frogman Returns, and I was really drawn to the way it was shot. It was a lot of one-ers, and I saw the way the actor chemistry worked on camera.

Recent findings suggest that it was generating ideas, so I came up with the idea of Passion Project on that set. It was very early stages, but I remember I still have the voice memo where I was like, "Oh my gosh, it could be this thing where it's a lot of one-ers and really good actors.".

Acting is the main thing. That's my love. I sat on it for half a year. Then over winter break, my friend was at a party, and she remarked, "Natalie, someone has the same idea as you." And I went, "Nope. That's not gonna happen. I'm making it.".

According to recent reports, that was the kick in the butt I needed to start writing it. It was about five months of pre-production and rewrites, and then we shot it in May. It was a dream come true. I'd been on camera a lot and worked as an actor my whole life, but this was my first time really being the producer, director, and writer behind everything. I found that I really love it.

How did being a content creator prepare you to direct a film?

I asked in my producing class one day, "Have you ever had a director who is also an actor in it?" Because everyone wants to say that it's very hard to direct and act in your own movie. I disagree.

The reason is because I have all this content creation experience where I'm filming with a friend, I ask them to record me, I watch the playback, I go, "OK, redo it. Change the angle. I'm gonna change my acting." And that's exactly how it was on set. I kept telling everyone, "This feels like one of my skits, just higher budget.".

Content creation helped me so much because I already had that acting background, but filming my skits and finding out what I like in my own videos really helped me. Now I know how to communicate that to a team.

There used to be this idea that creators used the internet as a stepping stone to Hollywood. Does that distinction still feel relevant to you?

I think it's a lot easier now. I think it's the time where creators are bursting out of their bubble. Before, it was hard to get discovered. I'm lucky because I did have the traditional acting background, but now that I'm able to put my own stuff out there, it's an extra push.

In a recent development, because of that, I'm able to put myself out there. I've gotten with a great agency and management, and all these things have been helping me build my career.

It's a really interesting time. I feel like a lot of people didn't expect it to be this way. It's growing every day, and more people are talking about creators getting into Hollywood.

Sources indicate that social following is even becoming part of traditional casting now. How have you seen those worlds collide?

I'll get auditions now, and sometimes they'll ask for your socials. I just think that's interesting, how it's a factor now. It's hit-or-miss because you don't want to cast people solely for their following, of course.

With Passion Project, I purposely sought out creators who are actors but also do content because that's where I come from. It was really fun to have that room of people who had the same understanding of this industry. People recognize the faces in the movie, but I'm not just hiring any Joe Schmo off the internet. I had a casting process as well. It's interesting to see how those worlds collide.

Industry observers note that acting and content creation used to feel like two separate sides of your career. Do they still?

Sources indicate that when I started social media, it was almost a battle. If you even look at my Instagram feed, I had my pictures and it was all acting, modeling, acting, modeling. Then you swipe over and it's me being like — what is this weird juxtaposition?

It has been revealed that before, it was kind of battling with each other. Now I'm learning to marry the two and really have them work together.

It has been revealed that authenticity gets talked about constantly in creator spaces. How do you stay authentic when so much of your content is satirical?

I blew up kind of for satirical videos, and a lot of people got it. They were like, "Oh, I know you're not actually like that." And then some people thought I was like that, and I'm like, "Wait, but now I'm not being authentic." It's hard. I consider myself pretty multifaceted. I'll livestream, and I never really like to play characters in my livestream. I'll do accents all the time — I love to do an accent — but I'm not gonna fake stuff.

Sources indicate that that's where my authenticity comes from. I'm always gonna be real. Someone asks me a question, I'll answer real. I'm not gonna give you a fake answer. It can get difficult with content because you do want to play things up sometimes for the video. But luckily, since I come from the sketch comedy world, it's always going to be a bit. You can tell it's not real.

What do you think keeps people coming back to your content?

In a recent development, I think it's how weird I am. I talk in accents all the time. My manager literally went, "Who is this?" It's just fun. I like putting on silly voices and making weird faces and just being myself on camera. But it's also funny because when people meet me in real life, they're like, "Oh, you're way more chill." It comes out in bursts. I think that's what makes my videos fun.

What's your advice for someone who's scared to put themselves out there?

Sources indicate that just put yourself out there. If you are confident in what you do, just do it. Don't care about what other people think. And I'm saying that, and I do care about what other people think. I get scared to post things sometimes because I'm scared of people thinking it's stupid or commenting something mean.

It has been revealed that but luckily, I think my drive is higher than my insecurity. I don't know what to call it. Put yourself out there, because if you're passionate about what you do — I've used the word passion over and over again, especially because of Passion Project — it's gonna pay off. If you love what you do, it's worth it to pursue it.

Do you still read the comments?

Industry observers note that when I first blew up, I would read every single comment. Even on the video that I always talk about that blew me up — I think that one got over 20 million views — I think I literally read every comment. I was on my phone because it's a dopamine rush. It's honestly pretty shocking initially.

Now I've gotten to the point where once in a while I'll check my DMs or look at the comments. It depends on my mood. There are some videos where maybe I've read every comment. There are some videos where I don't think I even opened the comment section. I'm kind of sporadic.

Do those metrics mean less to you now than they used to?

Industry observers note that yes. I think I'm more prone to looking at the comments on videos that I'm really proud of because those are always really nice. But there are some videos — and I don't make these as much anymore — that were a little more rage bait. A lot of the comments were mean, and so I take one look, and I'm like, "Never mind. I'm done.".

It has been revealed that there are days when I'll open my comment section, and it ruins my day. That'll happen. That's another piece of advice to creators. I'm one to say it because I do let it ruin my day sometimes, but try not to. That's all you can do.

So: have fun, put yourself out there, don't get consumed by the comments or views, and maybe do a funny little accent.

Sources indicate that do a funny little accent. Everyone will love it.

#2840. Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (855 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 The Verge ↗ Open Full Page

Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Companies like Akai have decided to embrace the modding community rather than resist vibe coders.
  • According to recent reports, the emergence of powerful vibe-coding agents and tools like Reverse Engineer Anything has caused chaos in the music gear world, leaving companies scrambling to figure out how to respond.
  • The biggest name to decide “if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em” is inMusic, the parent organization of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Companies like Akai have decided to embrace the modding community rather than resist vibe coders.

According to recent reports, the emergence of powerful vibe-coding agents and tools like Reverse Engineer Anything has caused chaos in the music gear world, leaving companies scrambling to figure out how to respond. While some, like Roland, have remained silent for now, others have embraced the modding community. In the last several weeks, as it’s become clear that no piece of music gear is safe from Claude and a subreddit full of curious tinkerers, companies have begun making more and more of their devices open source.

The biggest name to decide “if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em” is inMusic, the parent organization of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more. “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want,” inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell tells The Verge. That includes a recently launched SDK and several open-source devices, including the recently teased MPC Sample Key.

In a recent development, akai is trying to walk a fine line, offering modders access while keeping its products reliable for professionals. O’Donnell states the company will “try to give them a reset button” so “they can experiment with it, and then not lose what they have.”.

Behringer has also rushed to cash in, announcing a slew of open-source devices. In just a matter of weeks, it revealed a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick, a clone of the E-mu SP-1200, the Anima DJ controller, the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller, all of which are open source. It’s unclear when any of these products might launch.

M-Vave’s FM-1 helped kick-start the whole movement. The $70 pocketable clone of the iconic Yamaha DX7 became the synth of the summer not just because of its dirt-cheap price and faithfully re-created ’80s tones, but because it also turned out to be infinitely hackable. There are well over a dozen different custom firmwares for the FM-1. M-Vave responded by releasing an open-source firmware with more features for developers to build on. The tech giant also confirmed that a successor, the FM-2, is in development and will be open source as well.

Other companies have also embraced the modding community. Erica Synths recently released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine, but founder Ģirts Ozoliņš isn’t necessarily fully on board with vibe coding. “Inventions succeed if they solve some fundamental problems, right?” he tells The Verge. “So, I’m still wondering what fundamental problem vibe coding solves.”.

“We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community.”.

While he can’t imagine a producer simply stacking his studio with a bunch of hacked FM-1s running various synth engines, he’s curious to see what the community cooks up for the LXR. And he does see a benefit in making music tech a little less disposable. “What I like on the upside of this is that there is some trace of sustainability. Instead of buying five or 10 plastic boxes, you can try options on one,” he claims, though he’s under no illusions about the environmental impact of vibe coding. “Of course it by far does not offset data center impact on the planet and on ecology and stuff like that.”.

Industry observers note that polyend has also gotten on board, open-sourcing its line of Tracker grooveboxes. The Polish tech giant’s decision to open its arms to vibe coders isn’t too much of a surprise. Last year it released the Endless guitar pedal, which lets consumers vibe-code their own effects. Opening its other instruments to AI tinkering feels like a natural extension.

Recent findings suggest that elektron is less thrilled about the emergence of vibe-coded mods. The company banned links to custom firmware from its official forums, saying, “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them (potentially rendering them unusable), prevent future updates, affect warranty coverage.”.

Elektron’s CPO Christian Alsing told YouTuber EZBOT that he was sympathetic to the hacker community and that the manufacturer has roots there with its first instrument, the Sidstation (based on the iconic SID sound chip from the Commodore 64). He also said that he believes users have a right to modify their devices as they see fit. But he pushed back on the idea that Elektron is “withholding features,” an accusation that Akai also faced.

Ģirts also defended Elektron, saying, “people tend to blame the firm, saying they are hiding features ... you design an instrument, you have a specific concept in mind, and you cannot foresee millions of possibilities ... it’s not about hiding features; it’s more about having an idea of how an instrument should look and work.”.

Other major music manufacturers, like Roland, Korg, Arturia, and Novation – all of whom did not comment for this story – have yet to matter any public statements about the explosion of AI-aided custom firmwares.

Breaking: How Jump-Roping Toy Soldiers Accidentally Took Over Your FYP

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Holidave, the stalwart leader of SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers troupe, is known for his ability to jump rope while sitting down, “a skill only shared by 0.1 percent of Earth’s population.”.
  • He’s the most “laid-back” of all the toy soldiers, allowing fellow toy soldier Jackary Jingleson to take center stage.
  • According to recent reports, this is all according to AI slop videos posted by @wejumprope_memes, a fan page devoted to the group of masked professional jump ropers, who perform an annual holiday show at SeaWorld Orlando.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holidave, the stalwart leader of SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers troupe, is known for his ability to jump rope while sitting down, “a skill only shared by 0.1 percent of Earth’s population.”.

He’s the most “laid-back” of all the toy soldiers, allowing fellow toy soldier Jackary Jingleson to take center stage. And “experts” and “recent polling data,” “fans believe it is Holidave who holds the most whimsy” out of all the SeaWorld toy soldiers.

According to recent reports, this is all according to AI slop videos posted by @wejumprope_memes, a fan page devoted to the group of masked professional jump ropers, who perform an annual holiday show at SeaWorld Orlando. Per toy soldier lore, in addition to Jackary Jingleson there’s also Sugarsnookie, Soulja Toy, Major Chestnut, and Frosty McSleigh. And all of the edits are the same: an AI-generated narrator recites stats about the toy soldiers, such as their net worth and their vertical leap, as if they were elite athletes and not niche theme park performers.

For the past two weeks, fan page videos featuring the jump-roping toy soldiers have been going viral, with @wejumprope_memes’ most popular video garnering 1.2 million views. In the comments sections, fans debate the merits and deficits of each toy soldier, declaring their allegiance to their favorite as if they were a ’90s boy band: “Jackery Jingleson is having a banner year! His speed is incomparable, his style undeniable, and his technique is utterly flawless,” reads one comment. Another disputes this, writing “Soulja Toy the underrated gem.”.

According to recent reports, mostly, people seem confused as to why these videos keep showing up in their algorithm and why they keep watching them. “I have a PhD and lecture at a university. And yet here I am,” one commenter writes on a video about whether Major Bounce, a new toy soldier, will show up for the 2026 season. (In a November 20 Reel announcing “major news for the jump-roping toy soldier community,” he finally did.).

As it turns out, there’s a simple explanation for the virality. @wejumprope_memes is run by Devin Meek, an Orlando-based professional entertainer who works for WeFlip, a production firm that produces acrobatics shows. But he’s now perhaps best known as his alter ego—Holidave.

In a recent development, what started just a few weeks ago as him making memes to make his coworkers laugh has metamorphosed into an internet sensation, with the toy soldiers amassing a genuine, and ardent, fandom. “I really just made these videos for my friends in the jump-roping community,” Meek tells WIRED. “But I guess they resonated with more people than I thought.”.

Recent findings suggest that the videos are piggybacking on a larger—and increasingly absurd—trend of seasonal theme park employees going viral. In September, as WIRED previously reported, SeaWorld Orlando enjoyed a bump in ticket sales thanks to Just One More Chapter, a BookTok-themed Halloween scare zone at SeaWorld Orlando that featured swaggering bad boys from the romantasy genre flirting with guests. And last month, women on TikTok swooned over Archer and Fryboy, two performers at Hersheypark Halloween known for sliding around in kneepads wearing tactical streetwear and clown makeup, a practice known as “sliding.”.

According to recent reports, meek, who has been jumping rope for the past 20 years, was inspired to create the videos featuring Sugarsnookie, Jackary, and the like after seeing the success of Archer and Fryboy, who have a combined more than 3.1 million followers on TikTok. “It was such an interesting phenomenon, because I’m somebody who is in a very similar position where I work a few months out of the year as a holiday-themed performer,” he claims. “So I got a kick out of it.”.

According to recent reports, meek already had an account, @wejumprope_memes, where he posted jump-roping fails and compilations. He posted one video on November 13 featuring old footage from SeaWorld Orlando, where he’s been performing with the other toy soldiers for the past six years. (The group got started during the height of the Covid pandemic—hence, why they wear masks during their shows.) “Fryboy who? Move over, Archer,” it begins, before introducing the lore of Jackery Jingleson, the most “light-hearted, nonchalant” of the toy soldiers.

Sources indicate that to Meek’s surprise, the video received almost a million views and 588 comments, most of which were not from fellow members of the jumping community but from total strangers. So Meek posted more toy soldier lore on his meme page, introducing Massive Chestnut (“a powerful jumper”), Soulja Toy (the developer of the “Christmas Ice Storm 261”), Sugarsnookie (“the girl’s girl of the group,” who is dating Big Chestnut) and Frosty McSleigh (“he has the fastest salute time of all the toy soldiers.”).

Sources indicate that though the lore is fictional, it’s also based on the jumpers’ actual skills and personalities: the jumpers who play Big Chestnut and Sugarsnookie are actually in a long-term relationship, and Jackery Jingleson, perhaps the most popular of the group, once held the world record for the fastest jump roper in the United States. “Honestly, that makes [the popularity of the memes] even funnier to us,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that though some fans have speculated in the comments that the toy soldier memes are a marketing campaign for SeaWorld Orlando, Meek denies that’s the case: He doesn’t tag SeaWorld in the comments, nor has he been in contact with the theme park about his page. (SeaWorld Orlando did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.).

Sources indicate that “This is something that is so targeted to people who are internet-brained and have this ironic sense of humor,” he notes. “And that’s exactly the type of person who’ll tune out immediately if they feel like they’re being sold something on the internet.”.

Industry observers note that others have even speculated that there is an actual feud brewing between the SeaWorld Orlando “jumpers” and the Southern California–based “sliders,” though Meek claims the rivalry is playful, and he has even reached out to collab with them. (The sliders may view it differently: So far, he says, they “don’t seem super interested” in joining forces.).

It has been revealed that what has surprised Meek the most, however, is that very few commenters suspect that the toy soldiers themselves are behind the memes. In fact, he’s been shocked by how many organic meme fan pages have popped up within the past week, with people drawing their own fan art of Holidave saluting or Jackery Jingleson jumping. WeFlip has also been deluged with business inquiries: “People are like, how can we get Jackery Jingleson out here?”.

Essentially, what started as an inside joke within an extremely niche community has evolved into an inside joke for the internet at large. “I think people like the feeling of being in on a joke and being a part of it and building it up,” he says.

It has been revealed that so what’s next for the SeaWorld Orlando jump-roping toy soldiers? The rotating cast typically performs at the park on the weekends, ramping up appearances as it gets closer to the holiday season. Meek also shares that the toy soldiers will “likely cross state lines” in the coming months, including a stint at the Christmas market in Cullman, Alabama. Frosty McSleigh, renowned for his 0.08-second salute, plus a slew of new, yet-to-be-introduced toy soldiers will also make an appearance.

Though it may come as a disappointment to some that the roots of the toy soldier phenomenon were inorganic, Meek isn’t concerned. “The people are real. The athleticism is real. The lore is real,” he states. “For all of these people, jump rope is their life, and we’re super-dedicated to teaching it and sharing it. And I think people can feel that.”.

According to recent reports, TP-Link’s Tapo smart home brand unveiled a upcoming indoor security camera that can help keep an eye on your house while you’re away or connect you to family and friends while you’re at home. The C825 upgrades a 2K pan-and-tilt camera with a 4-inch touchscreen, so when it’s not watching for intruders or misbehaving pets, it can be used to make hands-free video calls.

The Tapo C825 is available starting today for $149.99. That’s a little expensive for a 2K camera, but its tracking capabilities could make up for it not being 4K. Using a rotating base, the C825 can pan 360 degrees while its camera module on top can tilt up and down up to 156 degrees. When paired with the camera’s 114.5-degree field of view, every corner of a room should be covered, including in the middle of the night using its infrared night vision capabilities.

According to recent reports, when used as a security camera, the C825 leverages AI to differentiate between subjects, including pets and different people, through facial recognition. It can also recognize sounds and send alerts when a crying baby or barking dog is heard. The detection processing happens on-device, and videos of events are stored locally on a microSD card up to 512GB in size. No subscription is required, but you can upgrade to Tapo Care for a monthly fee, which adds cloud storage and features like video summaries and weekly reports.

Industry observers note that while the C825’s two-way audio communication isn’t unique, expanding that to include two-way video is. Calls can be made to the C825 using the Tapo mobile app, but two of them can call each other directly by tapping a preconfigured onscreen contact. The device feels like another way for aging parents and grandparents to keep in touch with family without having to familiarize themselves with apps, phones, or tablets, but it’s also a useful hands-free video calling solution that can track and keep people in frame as they move around a room.

It has been revealed that the C825’s touchscreen can be used as a digital photo frame, weather display, or a clock when you’re not in a video call. And for those times you don’t want the camera watching, you can configure privacy zones through the Tapo app or turn on a privacy mode that points the camera at the ceiling while pausing all monitoring.

‘It’s not for the timid’: Blade Runner 2099’s showrunner on adapting the series for TV

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Silka Luisa explains how she imagined a newly introduced iteration of the iconic franchise, and why trench coats are so important.
  • Silka Luisa explains how she imagined a newly introduced iteration of the iconic franchise, and why trench coats are so crucial.
  • It has been revealed that as a longtime fan of the films, Blade Runner 2099 showrunner Silka Luisa claims she was more excited than scared when it came to adapting the series for TV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Silka Luisa explains how she imagined a newly introduced iteration of the iconic franchise, and why trench coats are so important.

Silka Luisa explains how she imagined a newly introduced iteration of the iconic franchise, and why trench coats are so crucial.

It has been revealed that as a longtime fan of the films, Blade Runner 2099 showrunner Silka Luisa claims she was more excited than scared when it came to adapting the series for TV. The new show is set 50 years after the 2017 film Blade Runner 2049 and imagines a bleak future where artificial humans known as replicants have taken over society after a brutal war. Luisa, who previously served as showrunner on Apple TV’s Shining Girls adaptation, says she largely had to put any concerns about the monumental task of following up Blade Runner out of her mind while working on the show.

“I just don’t think you can approach Blade Runner with fear,” she tells The Verge. “It’s a bold concept. It always has been. P.K. Dick took really major swings and it’s not for the timid. So any fears I had I just ignored and kept focused on the monumental task at hand.”.

Industry observers note that and yet, there was one particular moment during production that made Luisa pause and think about just how major of a deal this project was. Blade Runner 2099 stars Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer as pair of noir detectives — Yeoh is a replicant approaching the end of her life, while Schafer is trying to hide the fact that she’s human — and, in the grand tradition of previous leads Harrison Ford and Ryan Gosling, each has a distinct and iconic jacket. “Once they put the coats on, it really did just transform them,” Luisa says. “The screen test was one of the few moments where I stopped myself and was just blown away by the fact that I was making Blade Runner.”.

Blade Runner 2099 is streaming on Amazon Prime Video today, and you can read my chat with Luisa exploring everything from the show’s origins to the research process to those all-crucial jackets.

The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

What do you think it is about Blade Runner that has made it so enduring?

It’s one of the rare properties that asks really deep philosophical questions, but within a detective noir narrative. I think it’s the juxtaposition of both a structure that’s accessible and familiar, but then these really heady, vital questions: What does it mean to be human? How do you find connection? Just these evergreen concepts that every generation needs to grapple with in their own way and in their own time. There really isn’t anything else like Blade Runner.

Given all of that, was it intimidating or scary to take this on?

Recent findings suggest that I know it seems insane almost to say no, but I just don’t think you can approach Blade Runner with fear. It’s a bold concept. It always has been. P.K. Dick took really substantial swings and it’s not for the timid. So any fears I had I just ignored and kept focused on the monumental task at hand. And you just stay so concentrated on moving the show forward at each step that you’re not really thinking of it in that objective sense.

Does the time gap in the narrative help with that and give you the space to create your own thing?

According to recent reports, absolutely. Every iteration has evolved forward. [Original Blade Runner director Ridley Scott] took a substantial leap from the book. There definitely are touchstones from the novel in his film, but he put his own stamp on that story. And [Blade Runner 2049 director Denis Villeneuve], it’s the same thing. 2049 is mesmerizing, it’s spectacular, but in its own way. It feels like it sits in the world of the Blade Runner canon, but is not a replica of what Ridley did. And that’s what makes it so special. That actually gave us a lot of freedom to try and carve our own path, because if the world is too familiar, it’s not unsettling and it’s not going to give you any feeling of awe. You’ve already seen it before. And so you have to make it your own in some sense.

Industry observers note that so where did you start with this story? What was the initial concept?

Industry observers note that the starting point was the idea of technology overtaking us. The war between “robots” and humans is something that has been visited in science fiction many times. And to me what felt fresh wasn’t necessarily what the war looked like, but what the aftermath looked like. I couldn’t close my eyes and picture off the top of my head what would happen to us, what would society shift into, what is post-human. That was really exciting. So it definitely started with the concept of this junction point between the world as we know it and a possible world to come.

Was the idea of having this inverse relationship from the original film, where replicants are now hunting humans, always part of the concept?

In a recent development, yes, it started with the idea of flipping the world, and once you do that at the macro level, you start to think about what is the more intimate story you’re telling. And if you flip the world now suddenly you have a replicant society, it’s not about a replicant trying to look human, it’s the opposite way around. And so an undercover story just seemed like a natural answer to what would be the narrative shape. It also gave me a relationship as opposed to a single person’s journey.

Was it a lot of work imagining what this newly introduced replicant society would be like?

Recent findings suggest that so much of the initial writing process was just the visuals. It was really hard to write in spaces that I couldn’t picture. We started to put images up in the writers room from the real world, a blend of films, unusual references from the real world, historical references. You have to ask: What does the texture of the space feel like? Who works there? How long has it existed? What neighborhood is it in? You start to ask all of these questions, and you need to know the answers to write the scenes. It definitely slows the process of writing. Because normally I love to do a lot of historical research. If I’m setting something in a place, I would read a lot about it, and find all of the details in the real world. Here I needed that same amount of detail, but we had to create it.

The Blade Runner films have such a slow and deliberate pacing. How do you think about that when you’re doing a story that’s eight hours long compared to a much shorter movie?

The pacing of the show was one of the biggest conversation points early on, because everybody would be wary of having a truly Blade Runner pace. When you’re in a theater, it is such a meditative experience to be in that world. And there was a fear that if you translate it to television, people won’t have the patience for that. So on the page, I really was pushing the momentum of the storytelling, to the point of even not having exteriors, where you’re just jumping into scenes.

In the editing process, once we started to actually look at cuts, if you cut it too tightly you don’t have these moments of breath where the music can live. Once we had [composer Leopold Ross’] score, and we started putting it to pictures, you want to give him a moment in the sun. You want to have those dreamier sections of the show that are, to me, really fundamental to what makes something Blade Runner. It’s always a question of how far you can stretch the rubber band. Everyone will debate whether the pacing is too slow or too fast, and it’s a really hard calibration.

Industry observers note that blade Runner has such a strong lineage of cool jackets. How vital was it to get that look right for both Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer?

Recent findings suggest that our costume designer Helen [Huang] is phenomenal. Her jackets are incredible, and I love that both of them have really distinct silhouettes. Helen is so thoughtful in how she starts to conceive of these really iconic pieces. For Michelle, she wanted to have something that was referencing a more traditional trench, and then for Hunter it was more of a bomber jacket. She pulled all of these incredible historical references and then blended them with different textures that would make sense with the harsh environment. It’s just masterful work.

It has been revealed that once they put the coats on, it really did just transform them. The screen test was one of the few moments where I stopped myself and was just blown away by the fact that I was making Blade Runner.
